Ubi est Lūsitānia? Longēne abest? — Where is Portugal? Is it far away? (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
Sintram īmus. — We’re going to Sintra. (Fābula I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
Scīsne, Theodōre, quid sit obrigado? Lūsitānī ita grātiās agunt. — Do you know, Theo, what obrigado is? That’s how the Portuguese say thank you. (Fābula IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).

english: Spa / baths / sauna / steam room / hot tub / changing room
latin: thermae, thermārum f. · sūdātōrium, sūdātōriī n.
keywords: spa wellness baths bath house thermal springs sauna steam room hot room cold plunge jacuzzi whirlpool hot tub changing room

items.html: balneum (balineum), balneī n. — bath, bathroom; balneae, balneārum f. — public baths, a bath complex; thermae, thermārum f. — hot baths, a large bathing establishment, natural or artificial (Plin., Mart.). A modern spa is naturally thermae or balneae.
aquae, aquārum f. — mineral springs, a spa town: ad aquās venīre, go to the spa (Cic. Planc. 65; L&S); hence Aquae Sextiae (Aix) and Aquae Mattiacae (Wiesbaden).

sūdātōrium, sūdātōriī n. — sauna, sweating room (Traupman 374). Seneca defines it: sūdātōriīs, in quae siccus vapor corpora exhausūrus inclūditur — “sweating rooms, where dry heat is shut in to drain the body” (Ep. 51.6). Also assa, assōrum n. — dry sweating room (Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.2), and Lacōnicum, Lacōnicī n. — dry-heat room (Cic. Att. 4.10.2; Vitruvius).

caldārium, tepidārium, frīgidārium — the hot, warm and cold rooms of a bath (Vitruvius, Seneca, Pliny’s letters). The lexicon also uses frīgidārium for refrigerator (Traupman); the bath sense is the ancient one.

apodytērium, apodytēriī n. — changing room (Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.2; Plin. Ep. 5.6.25); ūnctōrium, ūnctōriī n. — oiling room (Plin. Ep. 2.17.11); lābrum, lābrī n. — basin, tub: lābrum sī in balineō nōn est, ut sit (Cic. Fam. 14.20.1).
balneum verticōsum — whirlpool, hot tub, jacuzzi (M-O s.v. whirlpool).
Hodiē in thermās īmus. — We’re going to the spa today.
In sūdātōriō nimis calidum est. — It’s too hot in the sauna.
Post sūdātōrium in piscīnam frīgidam dēsiliāmus! — After the sauna, let’s jump into the cold pool!

items.html: vēndō, vēndere, vēndidī, vēnditum — sell (Traupman 131; from vēnum dō); vēnditāre — keep offering for sale; vēnditor, vēnditōris m. — seller (Traupman 131; Cic.).
cārus, cāra, cārum — expensive (Traupman 130; M-O); percārus — very expensive (Ter. Phorm. 3.3.25, as cited by L&S); pretiōsus — costly, valuable.
magnī (parvī) cōnstāre — cost a lot (little) (Traupman 130, genitive of price); M-O magnō cōnstat, ablative. Both constructions are classical.
pretium facere or pretium statuere — set a price; mercis pretium inquīrere — ask the price (Traupman 130–131); M-O indicāre, name a price (Plaut.).

remissiō, remissiōnis f. — discount (Traupman 130); centēsima, centēsimae f. — one percent (Traupman 130; cf. classical centēsimae, one percent interest); pretium speciāle — a bargain, special price (Traupman 130).
omnia dīvēndita sunt — it’s all sold out (M-O; dīvendō, sell off piecemeal).
merx, mercis f. — an item, goods (Traupman 131); in lībrās — per pound (Traupman 131).
Hoc nimis cārum est. — This is too expensive.
Quantī hoc vēndis? — How much are you selling this for?
Haec māla parvī cōnstant. — These apples are cheap.

items.html: medicus, medicī m.; medica, medicae f. — doctor (Traupman 166).

items.html: tōnstrīx, tōnstrīcis f.; ōrnātrīx, ōrnātrīcis f. — hairdresser (Traupman 167, 325). Morgan–Owens gives tōnsor, tōnstrīx and capillōrum concinnātor (M-O s.v. barber, citing Col.). Classically tōnstrīx is a woman barber (Plaut.) and ōrnātrīx a lady’s maid who dressed her hair (Ov.).
tōnsor, tōnsōris m. — barber; tōnstrīna, tōnstrīnae f. — barber’s shop (Traupman 164, 173; Plaut.).
tōnsūra, tōnsūrae f.; tōnsus, tōnsūs m. — haircut (Traupman 164, 325); facere ut capillus tondeātur — get a haircut (Traupman 325).
fullō, fullōnis m. — dry cleaner; fullōnica, fullōnicae f. — dry cleaner’s, laundry (Traupman 166, 174, 338; Plaut.: the ancient fuller).
sūtor, sūtōris m. — shoemaker, cobbler; sūtrīna, sūtrīnae f. — shoemaker’s shop (Traupman 169; Plaut.).

vestificus, vestificī m.; vestifica, vestificae f. — tailor, dressmaker (Traupman 169; the Vatican lexicon gives vestifica); sarcinātor, sarcinātōris m.; sarcinātrīx, sarcinātrīcis f. — someone who alters and mends clothes (Traupman 169; Plaut.).
Crās ad tōnsōrem ībimus; capillī tuī nimis longī sunt. — Tomorrow we’ll go to the barber; your hair is too long.
Calceum ruptum ad sūtōrem ferāmus. — Let’s take the broken shoe to the cobbler.

items.html: police officer: Traupman gives vigil, vigilis m. (168); classically a member of the night watch, Rome’s police and fire brigade. Morgan–Owens gives pūblicae sēcūritātis custōs, and circitor for a patrolman (M-O s.v. policeman; patrolman).
sīphōnārius, sīphōnāriī m. — firefighter (Traupman 167; M-O s.v. fireman, from Egger; the Vatican lexicon agrees).

sacerdōs, sacerdōtis m./f. — priest (Traupman 169); bibliothēcārius, bibliothēcāriī m. — librarian (Traupman 167; late, Fronto); phōtographus, phōtographī m. — photographer (Traupman 53, 168; M-O s.v. photographer).
cantor, cantōris m. — singer (Hor. S. 1.3.1); Traupman gives cantātor and cantātrīx (169; cantātor is in Gellius).
babysitter, nanny: Morgan–Owens gives gerula, gerulae f. (Tert.; Apul.) and medieval cūnābulāria (M-O s.v. babysitter; nanny); the Vatican lexicon gives īnfantāria.
lorry driver: Traupman gives autocīnētī onerāriī gubernātor (219), Morgan–Owens plaustrārius (M-O s.v. truck-driver).
itinerum prōcūrātor, itinerum prōcūrātrīx — travel agent (Traupman 169, 219; the Vatican lexicon agrees).
Sīphōnāriī ignem exstinguunt. — The firefighters are putting out the fire.
Vigil nōbīs viam mōnstrābit. — The police officer will show us the way.
